result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B is the better answer, mainly because it handles embedded Latin stop names more convincingly. It puts the Latin face first in each script's stack and uses one designed-together family (Noto), so stop names inside Arabic and Japanese match in weight and size. It is also more open about what it hasn't verified and about platform fallbacks, and stays closer to typeface decisions. A is technically rich, with metric overrides and a per-script `lang` setup, but drifts into general RTL layout, icon mirroring and severity design. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A picks one coordinated family (Noto) for all three scripts and puts the Latin face first in each stack. That directly answers the question of making embedded Latin stop names match the surrounding weight and size. A also hedges honestly about licensing and coverage, and says to test with the fonts blocked. B covers more script-specific detail, such as Arabic letter-spacing, Han glyph variants and line-break rules, but it mixes Inter with other script faces without saying how to match their weights. It also drifts into general bidi, icon-mirroring and alert-hierarchy layout advice, and gives less clear guidance on system-font gaps.
